<title>Starship’s first orbital flight put its heat shield to the test – how it fares could determine if SpaceX’s vision is possible</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762534/original/file-20260928-50-9j5kzw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7920%2C5280&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">SpaceX&#39;s Starship rocket launched to orbit for the first time on Sept. 28, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SpaceXStarshipLaunch/59d7a49e0f35496184837d8fb3070549/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=spacex%20starship&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Eric Gay</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>SpaceX’s Starship, the <a href="https://theconversation.com/spacex-launches-most-powerful-rocket-in-history-in-explosive-debut-like-many-first-liftoffs-starships-test-was-a-successful-failure-204248">most powerful launch vehicle</a> ever developed, <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/28/science/live-news/spacex-starship-flight-14-launch">reached Earth orbit</a> for the first time on Sept. 28, 2026. This mission, the rocket’s 14th test flight, also marked the first time that Starship deployed <a href="https://www.space.com/spacex-starlink-satellites.html">Starlink internet satellites</a> into the existing larger constellation: 26 new next-generation nodes in total. </p>

<p>But not all went as planned. An engine went out, though SpaceX quickly determined Starship could still reach orbit without it. While SpaceX had planned for Starship to orbit the Earth six times, it changed gears and had Starship return after only two orbits. And the <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-science-behind-splashdown-how-nasa-got-the-artemis-ii-crew-safely-back-on-earth-232786">splashdown</a> in the Pacific Ocean ended in a huge bang, rather than the soft landing the company had hoped for.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/nouqj8wh_Kg?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">SpaceX’s Starship reenters the atmosphere and splashes down in the Pacific Ocean.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This flight can still be viewed as a success. It was an important step toward putting the enormous rocket to work by sending it into orbit. Starship is a key part of SpaceX’s vision. The company wants Starship to be a fully and rapidly <a href="https://www.spacex.com/mission">reusable transport system</a> that slashes the cost of spaceflight. </p>

<p>To realize <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-spacex-lowered-costs-and-reduced-barriers-to-space-112586">this vision of extremely low-cost launches</a>, SpaceX needs to be able to bring these spacecraft back from orbit, refurbish them and launch them again in short order.</p>

<p>Whether that all becomes quick and routine largely depends on dark ceramic tiles covering Starship’s underside. These tiles make up Starship’s <a href="https://theconversation.com/nasas-crew-capsule-had-heat-shield-issues-during-artemis-i-an-aerospace-expert-on-these-critical-spacecraft-components-245615">heat shield</a>.</p>

<p>I’m <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ckQTyHoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">an engineer and professor</a> who has researched the way <a href="https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2011-2284">heat shields respond when reentering the atmosphere</a>, a process that is extremely harsh on a spacecraft. I see Starship’s heat shield as a technical challenge that also drives the company’s economics. <a href="https://www.tweaktown.com/news/103616/elon-musk-reveals-the-biggest-problem-spacex-is-facing-with-starship/index.html">Elon Musk has agreed</a>.</p>

<p>A spacecraft that survives its return has passed an essential test. Next, engineers must establish how much work it will take to repair or replace the heat shield before its next launch. </p>

<h2>Why is reentry so difficult?</h2>

<p>A spacecraft in <a href="https://www.space.com/low-earth-orbit">low Earth orbit</a> travels at roughly 17,500 miles per hour (28,000 kilometers per hour). Returning to Earth means shedding an enormous amount of energy to slow down. Some shedding happens higher up by igniting the engine, but a lot of it happens lower down as the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Olihei-5q3M">spacecraft reenters through the atmosphere</a>. During reentry, strong <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/shock-wave">shock waves form</a> and heat up the surrounding atmosphere. Much of that heat transfers to the spacecraft.</p>

<p>If you’ve ever experienced a rug burn, you understand what is happening. You trip and your arm slides to a stop on a rug, with your bare skin experiencing a painful burn. If you were wearing a long-sleeved shirt, you might still feel the heat, but you would likely escape a severe burn.</p>

<p>The role of a spacecraft’s heat shield is similar to the protection that the shirt provides: It limits how much of that heat reaches the spacecraft structure underneath it. <a href="https://spacexstock.com/starship-heat-shield-how-it-handles-extreme-temperatures/">Starship’s heat shield</a> is composed of approximately 18,000 hexagonal tiles made of silica ceramic. You can think of them like the ceramic lining of a furnace: The fire in the furnace is extremely hot, but the tiles contain that heat.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A close of up the tip of the Starship rocket, which looks like a cone, with one side covered in a grid of hexagonal tiles." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762873/original/file-20260929-50-6006ms.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The dark, hexagonal tiles on Starship’s exterior make up the spacecraft’s heat shield.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SpaceXStarshipLaunch/7f066bdfa0224de082dbc23e76d60331/photo?vs=true&amp;isSemanticSearch=true&amp;displayquery=starship%20heat%20shield&amp;currentItemNo=5&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Eric Gay</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>To be reusable, the heat shield must withstand the mechanical demands of launch, such as pressure and vibrations, as well as the <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11372232">challenges of space</a>, such as <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-space-made-of-an-astrophysics-expert-explains-all-the-components-from-radiation-to-dark-matter-found-in-the-vacuum-of-space-235402">exposure to a vacuum</a>. It should also withstand the repeated cycles of heating and cooling that the rocket experiences during flight.</p>

<p>How the tiles are attached and the spaces between them matter as much as the material itself. A tile that tolerates the heat does little good if it falls off. A gap that lets hot gas reach the structure underneath can lead to catastrophe, as in the <a href="https://www.nasa.gov/remembering-columbia-sts-107/">space shuttle Columbia accident</a> in 2003.</p>

<p>Before the flight, <a href="https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/spacex-starship-flight-14-first-orbital-launch/">SpaceX engineers made some changes</a> they wanted to test. They attached the tiles more securely in vulnerable areas. They also added measures that stop hot plasma from traveling behind tiles and added curved tiles to reduce heating in the gaps.</p>

<p>SpaceX also reflew two tiles recovered from a previous Starship. Repeating a flight with previously exposed material can test how the protection holds up over time. Two tiles, however, cannot establish how many flights an entire heat shield will last.</p>

<h2>What exactly does a successful return mean?</h2>

<p>SpaceX equipped <a href="https://openthemagazine.com/books/starship-flight-14-set-for-first-orbital-mission-carrying-26-starlink-v3-satellites">three of the Starlink satellites released on Monday with cameras</a> to inspect Starship’s heat shield after deployment. </p>

<p>Their images could tell engineers about any damage the ship took as it launched and entered orbit. This way, they can compare the photos to the tiles after reentry to learn about the heat shield’s performance. Engineers will look at where the damage occurred, what caused it and whether the same hardware could fly again safely. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A rocket flying through the sky, propelled by a streak of flame" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762586/original/file-20260928-60-yeedde.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Starship’s 14th test flight heads toward space on Sept. 28, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SpaceXStarshipLaunch/aca4bb599414457bb6a2e812154ac908/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=spacex%20starship&amp;currentItemNo=7&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Eric Gay</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The business case requires reusability</h2>

<p>The logic behind reusable rockets is straightforward: Spreading the cost of building a vehicle over many missions lowers the hardware cost for each launch.</p>

<p>But the <a href="https://spacexstock.com/reusable-rockets-vs-single-use-rockets-cost-breakdown/">accounting also includes</a> inspection, replacement parts, labor, propellant, ground facilities and the risk of losing a vehicle. A rocket waiting for repairs ties up capital.</p>

<p>My engineering assessment is that heat shield improvements can produce two kinds of savings: First, better heat shields require fewer repairs after each mission. And a more rapid turnaround time would allow each vehicle to fly more missions. This achievement could make reuse more valuable than simply recovering the expensive hardware from a used Starship, to be reinstalled on a new spacecraft.</p>

<p>SpaceX’s own <a href="https://content.spacex.com/cms-assets/FINAL_Documents%20and%20Updates/SpaceX%20-%20EU%20Prospectus%20(Approved%20by%20Bafin)%20-%20June%205,%202026.pdf">investor disclosures</a> make this connection explicit. They warn that failing to achieve full reuse and quick turnaround times between flights could increase launch costs. Delays could also stall the deployment of satellites in the Starlink constellation, which is a major source of revenue growth.</p>

<h2>Satellites, the Moon and data centers</h2>

<p>NASA also plans to use Starship on future missions to the Moon, which will require Starship to be ready for a sequence of launches.</p>

<p>A March 2026 <a href="https://oig.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/final-report-ig-26-004-nasas-management-of-the-human-landing-system-contracts.pdf">report from NASA’s inspector general</a> described a plan requiring more than 10 Starship tanker flights. These Starship tankers would carry propellant to lunar orbit, where each would rendezvous with, dock to and transfer propellant to a storage depot. However, NASA’s timeline for returning to the Moon is <a href="https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/">already facing delays</a>, and any delays with Starship could add further delay.</p>

<p>SpaceX has also proposed building <a href="https://theconversation.com/building-data-centers-in-space-is-an-intriguing-idea-on-paper-but-major-engineering-challenges-must-be-solved-284053">orbital data centers</a>, which would use Starship to launch the heavy computing satellites to orbit. But SpaceX’s prospectus says it will need Starship to be fully reusable for these plans to be economically attractive. </p>

<p>For me, the next telling milestone will be recovering a Starship and then inspecting it and preparing it to launch again. To date, SpaceX has successfully reused only its <a href="https://www.spacex.com/launches/starship-flight-9">first-stage Super Heavy booster</a>, not the Starship vehicle itself. SpaceX will need to show that this process is becoming predictable and routine. That feat would require a heat shield that protects both the spacecraft and the economics behind Starship.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292960/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

A gap that lets hot gas reach the structure underneath can lead to catastrophe, as in the space shuttle Columbia accident in 2003
Before the flight, SpaceX engineers made some changes they wanted to test
They attached the tiles more securely in vulnerable areas
They also added measures that stop hot plasma from traveling behind tiles and added curved tiles to reduce heating in the gaps
SpaceX also reflew two tiles recovered from a previous Starship
Repeating a flight with previously exposed material can test how the protection holds up over time

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762840/original/file-20260929-50-3q2qz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=79%2C101%2C2280%2C1520&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Members of the Tigray People&#39;s Liberation Front walk along a main road in Mekele, the regional capital of Tigray, on Sept. 23, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/members-of-the-tigray-peoples-liberation-front-walk-along-a-news-photo/2296131169?adppopup=true">AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Four years after a fragile ceasefire ended widespread conflict in Ethiopia, the region is again <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/29/fighting-in-ethiopia-intensifies-whats-the-latest">slipping back into full-out war</a>.</p>

<p>On Sept. 23, 2026, advancing soldiers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/23/ethiopian-airlines-suspends-flights-to-three-northern-tigray-airports">seized government positions</a> in northern Ethiopia.</p>

<p>It followed the announcement of a new <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/seven-ethiopian-armed-groups-announce-anti-government-alliance-2026-09-21/">alliance of seven</a> armed movements in opposition to the Ethiopian government and deteriorating relations between the country and neighboring Eritrea, which it <a href="https://apnews.com/article/ethiopia-tigray-war-eritrea-sudan-egypt-6b3208122a4221f3c2e8dcbe21630016">accuses of supporting the new alliance</a>.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://ccd.indiana.edu/staff-boards-fellows/graduate-fellows.html">expert on conflict in the Horn of Africa and Ethiopian national security</a>, I know the spiraling conditions now have been long in the making. The November 2022 Pretoria <a href="https://igad.int/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Download-the-signed-agreement-here.pdf">Cessation of Hostilities Agreement</a> ended immediate fighting between Ethiopia and Tigrayan rebels, but it <a href="https://theconversation.com/ethiopias-peace-deal-is-unravelling-what-went-wrong-with-the-tigray-agreement-293005">did not constitute a comprehensive peace settlement</a>. Crucially, it was never followed by wider political negotiations to address the root causes of the war. The concern now is that the conflicts will intersect with the civil war in neighboring Sudan, causing a complicated, regionwide conflagration.</p>

<h2>How has the conflict escalated?</h2>

<p>The Sept. 23 ground offensive by the TPLF drew global attention to the situation in Ethiopia. But in reality, the ratcheting up of tensions between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the TPLF has been going on for months.</p>

<p>Throughout August and September, the region of Tigray – Ethiopia’s northernmost constituent state, with an estimated population of roughly 7 million – has been subjected to federal air and drone attacks. Tigrayan organizations and <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/09/25/ethiopia-indiscriminate-airstrike-in-tigray">human rights groups</a> <a href="https://omnatigray.org/joint-statement-urgent-call-to-stop-the-renewed-war-on-tigray/">reported that</a> schools, residential areas, a farmer training center and a truck carrying food aid were all hit during the air campaign.</p>

<p><iframe id="7QAvy" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7QAvy/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of East Africa."></iframe></p>

<p>The strikes occurred amid mounting tensions over the TPLF’s <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/tigray-party-restores-pre-war-government-threat-northern-ethiopia-peace-2026-05-05/">restoration of the regional political administration</a> that preceded the 2020-2022 civil war, an incomplete disarmament of the group and <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/1/fighting-breaks-out-in-western-tigray-as-ethiopia-and-tplf-trade-blame">renewed localized clashes</a>. In short, the federal government accused Tigrayan forces of remobilizing; the apparent purpose of the federal attacks was to degrade Tigrayan military capability.</p>

<p>The federal government had also been squeezing the region economically, by <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/tigray-party-restore-pre-war-administration-jeopardising-northern-ethiopia-peace-2026-04-20/">withholding funds</a> needed to pay Tigray’s civil servants and limiting access to banks and fuel, according to the TPLF.</p>

<p>The situation escalated further on Sept. 20 when seven armed organizations announced the formation of the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/seven-ethiopian-armed-groups-announce-anti-government-alliance-2026-09-21/">Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival</a> in opposition to the federal government.</p>

<p>Three days later, Tigrayan forces began a <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/23/ethiopian-airlines-suspends-flights-to-three-northern-tigray-airports">coordinated ground operation</a> against federal positions at airports in the regional capital Mekele, along with two other Tigrayan cities, Axum and Shire. Fighting then spread along Tigray’s borders with the Amhara and Afar regions.</p>

<p>Federal forces mounted a counteroffensive, and on Sept. 28 pro-government forces <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/nation-world/world/article317408631.html">claimed to have entered Alamata</a> – an important transport and supply center south of Mekelle.</p>

<h2>Who are the main actors?</h2>

<p>Prime Minister <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/topics/c4wl7lwmw0qt">Abiy Ahmed</a>’s federal government and the Ethiopian National Defense Forces retain formidable advantages in the current conflict: a national professional army, combat aircraft and drones, and federal revenues.</p>

<p>Its main opponent in the north is <a href="https://www.armedgroups-internationallaw.org/2022/10/14/the-tigray-peoples-liberation-front-a-provincial-ruling-political-party-turned-into-a-rebel-government/">the TPLF</a>, which was the dominant organization in Ethiopia’s ruling coalition from 1991 until Abiy became prime minister in 2018. It remains the strongest organized political and military force in Tigray.</p>

<p>The most striking partnership in the new alliance is between the TPLF and the <a href="https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2024/11/12/who-fano-inside-ethiopia-amhara-rebellion">Fano movement in Amhara</a>, which fought alongside the federal army during the 2020–2022 civil war. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some of the alliance’s members have limited military capacity, and there remains serious disagreements over territory and political objectives.</p>

<p>Nevertheless, it has adopted a workable minimum program: removing Abiy’s government, establishing an inclusive transitional administration and undertaking constitutional reform. </p>

<p>For its part, Eritrea is the most important potential external actor. Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal military during the previous war and were accused of <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/military-history-and-science/atrocities-ethiopias-tigray-region/">atrocities against Tigrayan civilians</a>. Addis Ababa now <a href="https://www.rfi.fr/en/africa/20260928-ethiopia-accuses-sudan-eritrea-of-backing-tigray-forces-as-fighting-escalates">accuses Eritrea and Sudan</a> of backing the new alliance. Both countries deny the allegation.</p>

<h2>What is the wider background to the tensions?</h2>

<p>The conflict is rooted in an unresolved constitutional struggle over federalism, regional autonomy, territory and the distribution of political power.</p>

<p>After becoming prime minister in 2019, Abiy <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2019/12/5/why-abiy-ahmeds-prosperity-party-could-be-bad-news-for-ethiopia">dissolved the former ruling coalition</a> and created a new one that the TPLF declined to join.</p>

<p>Relations deteriorated further when Tigray held a regional election in 2020 after the federal government postponed national and regional elections. War began later that year.</p>

<p>Over the next two years, as many as 600,000 people may have died from violence, hunger and the collapse of health services, while <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/2f385e95-0899-403a-9e3b-ed8c24adf4e7">more than 2 million were displaced</a>.</p>

<p>The 2022 ceasefire agreement halted large-scale combat, but its political and security provisions <a href="https://theconversation.com/ethiopias-peace-deal-is-unravelling-what-went-wrong-with-the-tigray-agreement-293005">were never fully implemented</a>.</p>

<p>The TPLF began handing over heavy weapons in line with the accord, but further disarmament never happened as a result of a failure of Eritrean and other nonfederal forces to withdraw from parts of Tigray.</p>

<p>The agreement also required Tigray’s representation in federal institutions, including both houses of parliament. An inclusive interim regional administration was to be established until regional and federal elections could be held. </p>

<p>But that arrangement became effectively indefinite, with successive <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/ethiopias-pm-abiy-appoints-new-leader-tigray-administration-2025-04-08/">heads of Tigray’s interim administration</a> appointed by Abiy.</p>

<p>In 2025, the TPLF’s legal registration as a party about to compete in elections <a href="https://addisstandard.com/ethiopias-election-board-revokes-tplfs-legal-status/">was revoked</a>, and Tigray was excluded from Ethiopia’s June 2026 national vote. Tigray’s reintegration into Ethiopia’s federal institutions likewise remained incomplete.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the status of western and southern Tigray remained unresolved. <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/ethiopian-airlines-suspends-flights-tigray-region-2026-01-07/">Hundreds of thousands of displaced people</a> have <a href="https://www.refugeesinternational.org/just-security-in-ethiopia-an-unfinished-peace-risks-betraying-the-people-of-tigray-and-the-broader-region/">been unable to return</a> to these areas claimed by both Tigray and the Amhara region of Ethiopia.</p>

<p>So in part, the seeds to the conflict now were sown in the 2022 ceasefire. What was supposed to open the way to a comprehensive peace agreement instead hardened into a new and increasingly unstable status quo.</p>

<h2>How could this affect the wider region?</h2>

<p>The first danger is a direct confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea.</p>

<p>Relations between the two governments <a href="https://theconversation.com/ethiopia-and-eritrea-are-on-edge-again-whats-behind-the-growing-risk-of-war-276424">have deteriorated sharply</a> over the demand by Ethiopia, which is landlocked, to have access to the Red Sea. Statements from Ethiopian officials <a href="https://theconversation.com/ethiopia-eritrea-tensions-over-red-sea-port-have-turned-the-tigray-peace-deal-into-a-political-weapon-290096">contemplating the acquisition of the Eritrean port of Assab by force</a> have caused alarm in the Eritrean capital of Asmara.</p>

<p>Such rhetoric has contributed to the conditions under which Eritrea might decide to support Ethiopian armed groups now.</p>

<p>A direct Ethiopian-Eritrean war would transform an internal Ethiopian conflict into an interstate war along the Red Sea’s western hinterland, with potentially devastating effects. A war <a href="https://www.aaas.org/resources/ethiopian-occupation-border-region-eritrea-case-study-summary">between the two neighbors</a> between 1998 and 2000 <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-44004212">killed tens of thousands</a> and <a href="https://www.aaas.org/resources/ethiopian-occupation-border-region-eritrea-case-study-summary">displaced as many as 650,000 people</a> on both sides of the Eritrea-Ethiopia border.</p>

<p>The second danger is convergence with the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/sudan-war-156557">civil war in neighboring Sudan</a>. Ethiopia has accused Sudanese forces of supporting the TPLF and other Ethiopian armed groups; Sudan has denied the charge. </p>

<p>Sudan’s army, in turn, has accused Ethiopia of <a href="https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/sudan-rejects-claim-it-backs-ethiopian-opposition-vows-to-protect-sovereignty/4071104">assisting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces</a>, which have been fighting government forces for control of the country.</p>

<p>The risk is that Ethiopia’s conflict and Sudan’s war become mutually enabling. For example, Eritrea could support the armed alliance to deter the Ethiopian government from pursuing access to the sea through the Eritrean port of Assab. Sudan’s army could support the same groups to pressure Ethiopia to end its alleged backing of the Rapid Support Forces. Such involvement could provide armed organizations with cross-border bases, weapons and supply routes, widening both conflicts. </p>

<p>Egypt and Gulf Arab countries already involved in Sudan could likewise be drawn more deeply into the Ethiopian conflict.</p>

<p>The third danger concerns Ethiopia’s trade corridor through Djibouti. Ethiopia <a href="https://maritimebizreview.com/?p=2164">depends on Djibouti</a> for the overwhelming majority of its maritime commerce, including fuel imports. If fighting in Ethiopia’s Afar region threatens the highway and railway linking Addis Ababa to Djibouti, the conflict would have immediate national and international economic consequences.</p>

<p>For the United States, which has <a href="https://etbusinessview.com/2026/09/23/u-s-ambassador-condemns-tplf-offensive-as-fighting-erupts-across-tigray-afar-and-amhara/">blamed the TPLF for the escalation</a>, the stakes extend beyond humanitarian concerns. Ethiopia is one of Africa’s most populous countries, hosts the African Union and has long been an important U.S. security partner in the Horn.</p>

<h2>Can both sides return to the ceasefire?</h2>

<p>The agreement’s political framework has been overtaken by events, and Ethiopia’s conflicts are no longer confined to the relationship between Addis Ababa and Mekelle.</p>

<p>Preventing a wider war will, I believe, require an immediate halt to airstrikes and offensive ground operations, restoration of communications and humanitarian access, and independent investigations into attacks on civilians. It will also require negotiations toward the comprehensive political agreement that was supposed to follow the 2022 Pretoria agreement.</p>

<p>Those negotiations can no longer be limited to the federal government and the TPLF. They must address the wider alliance, other political constituencies, contested territories, regional representation and the future of Ethiopia’s federal system.</p>

<p>The question is no longer whether Addis Ababa and Mekelle can restore their former bilateral arrangement. It is whether Ethiopia can establish an inclusive constitutional process before its previously separate conflicts converge into a national and potentially regional war.</p>

<title>Chatbots as oracles: How AI is giving new life to the ancient practice of seeking answers from inscrutable sources</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762119/original/file-20260924-60-4acsdz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5700%2C3800&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People are turning to AI with life’s difficult questions and to glimpse into the future.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/robot-fortune-teller-hand-and-crystal-ball-royalty-free-image/1603248194?phrase=crystal%20ball%20ai&amp;adppopup=true">Yuichiro Chino/Moment via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>People are increasingly turning to AI for advice. A <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/americans-and-ai-2026-chatbots-smart-devices-and-views-on-impact">2026 Pew report</a> found that 10% of Americans are using chatbots for emotional support or companionship. Some even find a <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-ai-resembles-a-charismatic-religious-leader-291831">charismatic leader in AI</a>. </p>

<p>More broadly, <a href="https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w34255/w34255.pdf">a large-scale study of 1.1 million ChatGPT conversations</a> found that 49% of the messages involved users seeking “information or advice” to help them be “better informed or make better decisions.” </p>

<p>Their questions are not just about ordinary practical matters. In 2021, Ask Delphi, an AI-based website to which people could pose ethical or moral questions, received <a href="https://www.geekwire.com/2021/teaching-artificial-intelligence-right-from-wrong-new-tool-from-ai2-aims-to-model-ethical-judgments/">3 million queries</a> in a few weeks. The system’s <a href="https://www.geekwire.com/2021/teaching-artificial-intelligence-right-from-wrong-new-tool-from-ai2-aims-to-model-ethical-judgments/">designers – researchers at the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Washington – said</a> they did not intend it to be a moral authority but worried that users might see it that way.</p>

<p>The Verge, a technology news publication, <a href="https://www.theverge.com/2021/10/20/22734215/ai-ask-delphi-moral-ethical-judgement-demo">argued that the system’s name – Ask Delphi – encouraged users</a> to see the system as an inscrutable source of superior knowledge. It was named after the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Delphic-oracle">Delphic oracle</a> to whom ancient Greeks posed difficult questions. The oracle was a priestess who entered a trance state to convey answers from Apollo, the Greek god of prophecy.</p>

<p>The choice of “Delphi” is suggestive. Throughout history, when societies confront challenging questions, they have turned to sources believed to know more than any ordinary human could. Oracles, prophets and practices of divination offered guidance from inscrutable or enigmatic sources when ordinary human judgment reached its limits. </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/webbkeane/">anthropologist interested in religion</a> and an <a href="https://www.ambujtewari.com/">AI researcher interested in chatbots</a>, we are intrigued that the ancient idea of an oracle has resurfaced in discussions about conversational AI. Like ancient oracles, modern AI is increasingly consulted about difficult questions that exceed the judgment or knowledge of any individual – from “Is it OK to lie to protect someone’s feelings?” to “Exploding a nuclear bomb to save your child.”</p>

<p>But the resemblance does not stop there: The processes through which AI arrives at an answer are inscrutable not just to users but also to the designers of these systems. We argue that this opacity is part of the reason people perceive these systems as having authority. </p>

<h2>An ancient human predicament</h2>

<p>Oracles, whether humans like the priestess at Delphi or techniques like <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780190072452.001.0001">I Ching divination</a>, have appeared in societies from Ancient Greece to China and across religious traditions.</p>



<p>For example, <a href="https://www.drikpanchang.com/prashnavali/rama-shalaka.html">the Ram Shalaka oracle</a> is based on the Hindu scripture Ramcharitmanas, a 16th-century retelling of the ancient Indian epic Ramayana. A user places their finger on a random square in a 15-by-15 grid. A fixed counting procedure then reveals a verse from the scripture that is supposed to answer the question in the user’s mind. In <a href="https://www.ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=bibliomancy">Christian bibliomancy</a>, a form of divination, a person seeking guidance opens the Bible at random and interprets the passage they encounter as an answer to their question.</p>

<p>The use of randomness in these oracular techniques creates an enigmatic black box effect – no one can explain just how the chance element embedded in these techniques connects with the answer that emerges. Yet that opacity is part of the oracle’s authority. Users seeking transcendental sources of insight do not know or care how the oracle came up with its responses. </p>

<p>Anthropologists find that <a href="https://www.anthroencyclopedia.com/entry/divination">oracles and divination</a> commonly use techniques that generate <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/anoc.12006">random outcomes</a>. As a result, their answers seem disinterested and their sources enigmatic, reinforcing the perception that they are in touch with something beyond human limits.</p>

<p>Interestingly, the idea of the oracle entered computer science, acquiring a precise mathematical meaning in 1939. Alan Turing, whose ideas were foundational to both computer science and AI, adopted the concept in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-45.1.161">work based on his Ph.D. thesis</a>. He introduced “oracle machines,” mathematical models of computation that could consult an external source for answers unavailable to the machine itself. </p>

<p>In other words, in both mathematical and religious uses, an oracle provides answers to problems that could not be resolved within an existing system or set of axioms.</p>

<h2>The oracle in the age of AI</h2>

<p>Modern chatbots like ChatGPT are considered opaque black boxes. This is not because the full machinery behind their computations is hidden from users. The opacity claim applies even to <a href="https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions/what-is-an-open-weight-model">open-weight models</a>, whose numerical parameters, called “weights,” are publicly available.</p>

<p>The computations these models perform are elementary: additions, multiplications and simple mathematical functions. But an enormous number of such computations occur when answering a user query, making it nearly impossible to understand what the system is doing as a whole.</p>

<p>Crucially, the weights governing these computations are not individually designed by humans. They are learned automatically from internet-scale data during training. Even when the weights and every elementary computation are available for inspection, no one can readily understand how the models produce a particular answer. In fact, an entire area of modern AI, called “<a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/team/interpretability">mechanistic interpretability</a>,” is devoted to improving our understanding of how AI systems work internally.</p>

<p>Remarkably, the designers of AI systems acknowledge that they do not fully understand how their systems produce certain behaviors. Even when designers do not intend for their systems to be oracular, they can produce <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9655.70133">conversations that can seem religious</a>. </p>

<p>Last year, for example, Anthropic <a href="https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/6be99a52cb68eb70eb9572b4cafad13df32ed995.pdf">publicly reported</a> an unexpected phenomenon involving Claude 4. Normally, Claude converses with a human. Anthropic engineers instead placed Claude on both sides of a conversation. The machine-to-machine conversation quickly turned into discussions of consciousness and self-awareness, producing content with spiritual, metaphysical or poetic themes.</p>

<p>Anthropic called this puzzling behavior pattern <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-models-might-be-drawn-to-spiritual-bliss-then-again-they-might-just-talk-like-hippies-257618">the “spiritual bliss” attractor</a>, a tendency for the conversation to gravitate toward mystical topics. They emphasized that it was unexpected because it emerged without explicit training for such behaviors.</p>

<p>Our argument is not that ChatGPT is the new Delphic oracle, or that most people believe AI is divine. Nor are its answers infallible. Rather, the history of oracles points to an enduring feature of human life: Whenever we reach the limits of what we can determine for ourselves, we look beyond ourselves for answers. Today, AI is becoming one such source. The institutions may have changed dramatically over time – the human predicament has not.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289279/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Oil and gas industry expected surplus – but war brought shortage instead</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761807/original/file-20260923-50-cnd3z5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">With fuel prices at record highs, a truck driver prepares to pump diesel into a tractor trailer at a gas station in Florida.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/luis-torrado-pumps-diesel-fuel-into-his-tractor-trailer-at-news-photo/2294761154">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In 2023, the International Energy Agency predicted that by 2028 <a href="https://www.iea.org/news/growth-in-global-oil-demand-is-set-to-slow-significantly-by-2028">the world’s oil companies would produce more oil than people wanted to buy</a>. Prices responded to that and similar projections of slowing oil demand, <a href="https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/123125-commodities-2026-industry-calls-for-more-oil-but-capex-spending-sees-muted-growth">dropping too low to attract investment for new wells and refineries</a>. </p>

<p>No forecast anticipated that the <a href="https://theconversation.com/hormuz-closure-threatens-the-global-food-supply-why-grocery-price-hikes-are-coming-279899">Strait of Hormuz</a>, the main route for Middle Eastern oil to reach global markets, would be <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-shadow-tankers-are-the-only-ships-still-moving-through-the-strait-of-hormuz-277785">almost completely blocked</a>. </p>

<p>So in March 2026, when the strait closed in the wake of <a href="https://theconversation.com/at-a-glance-us-israel-attack-on-iran-277186">U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran</a>, there was little anyone could do to quickly restore the flow of oil and gas the world’s economy depends on. Some countries did have strategic reserves, but a <a href="https://theconversation.com/over-400-million-barrels-will-be-added-to-the-oil-market-soon-what-are-strategic-reserves-and-what-can-they-do-278370">massive coordinated release</a> from those supplies didn’t make a difference for long – and those reserves <a href="https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/oil-stocks-of-iea-countries">may need to be replenished</a>, paradoxically increasing demand for oil in the future.</p>

<p>Just before that conflict broke out, my fellow researcher, Hiroyasu Sakaguchi at the <a href="https://eneken.ieej.or.jp/en/">Institute of Energy Economics, Japan</a>, and <a href="https://experts.okstate.edu/john.schoeneman">I</a> wrote a <a href="https://hamminstitute.org/site-files/documents/tesc/PeakOilReport_accessibility_remediated.pdf">report on oil and gas demand forecasts</a> warning that even in the midst of oversupply, the global buffer for disruption is quite fragile. It was published by the <a href="https://hamminstitute.org/research/tesc">Trilateral Energy Security Committee</a>, which promotes energy-security cooperation between the U.S., Japan and South Korea.</p>

<p>As the fighting has continued, oil prices have climbed, <a href="https://theconversation.com/oil-shortages-escalate-from-wars-in-iran-and-ukraine-with-few-signs-of-relief-288858">causing fuel shortages</a> and raising prices not only of <a href="https://theconversation.com/whats-in-the-price-of-a-gallon-of-gas-281494">gasoline</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/iran-war-pushes-diesel-the-economys-lifeblood-to-record-high-prices-with-no-relief-on-the-horizon-292049">diesel</a>, but <a href="https://theconversation.com/hormuz-closure-threatens-the-global-food-supply-why-grocery-price-hikes-are-coming-279899">fertilizer, food</a>, consumer goods and <a href="https://theconversation.com/oil-isnt-just-fuel-iran-conflict-could-disrupt-markets-for-everything-from-plastics-to-fertilizers-277946">just about everything else</a>.</p>

<h2>What an oil forecast is</h2>

<p>The reasons today’s demand and supply are so mismatched took shape years earlier, in spreadsheets that most people don’t know about or ignore.</p>

<p>It can take <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/the-implications-of-oil-and-gas-field-decline-rates/executive-summary">about 20 years</a> to go from exploring a new oil or gas field to shipping petroleum from it. When companies, banks and governments are deciding what projects to invest in, they look for indicators of how much oil and gas the world will want a decade or more from now.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/ieo/">Government research agencies</a>, <a href="https://www.opec.org/assets/assetdb/woo-2025.pdf">oil-producing countries</a> and <a href="https://www.bp.com/en/global/corporate/energy-economics/energy-outlook.html">big oil and gas companies</a> all produce long-range projections of demand and supply. These projections are really sets of “what-if” stories. Forecasters start with how much energy the world uses today, then <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-outlook-2025/stated-policies-scenario">make assumptions</a> on topics such as how fast economies will grow, how quickly new technologies like electric cars will be adopted, and how policies like those on pollution and greenhouse gas emissions will change.</p>

<p>Each set of assumptions produces a different answer. When my colleagues and I <a href="https://hamminstitute.org/site-files/documents/tesc/PeakOilReport_accessibility_remediated.pdf">compared major projections from 2025 for 2035</a>, the highest projections expected 116.6 million barrels a day would be used; the lowest expected 89.4 million barrels a day. That’s an enormous difference of 27.2 million barrels a day just 10 years out, equal to about one-quarter of all the oil the world uses today.</p>

<p><iframe id="7swyh" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7swyh/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A line chart showing several different oil demand forecasts and how widely they vary."></iframe></p>

<h2>Forecasts don’t always pan out</h2>

<p>Oil forecasts a year or two out tend to be reasonably close to reality and each other, because most of the expected production is already in motion. But much like weather forecasts, the further into the future an oil market forecast looks, the more errors are possible, both with small errors in assumptions and big surprises nobody saw coming.</p>

<p>In the early 2000s, many experts worried the world was running out of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2018.09.022">oil that was cheap and easy to produce</a>. Then, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=37815">new drilling and hydraulic fracturing methods unlocked oil stored in layers of shale</a>. From 2008 to 2025, U.S. production rose from <a href="https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/leafhandler.ashx?n=pet&amp;s=mcrfpus2&amp;f=m">5 million barrels a day to 13.6 million</a>.</p>

<p>In 2022, the International Energy Agency’s main scenario had <a href="https://www.carbonbrief.org/iea-fossil-fuel-use-will-peak-before-2030-unless-stated-policies-are-abandoned">world oil demand peaking in the mid-2030s</a>. A year later, largely because sales of electric cars were increasing so quickly, the agency <a href="https://www.npr.org/2023/10/24/1207976763/global-shift-to-clean-energy-means-fossil-fuel-demand-will-peak-soon-iea-says">moved that peak to before 2030</a>. </p>

<p>Then in 2025, the IEA revived a scenario it had shelved – one counting only policies already in force – <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/world-energy-outlook-2025/current-policies-scenario">in which oil demand keeps rising until at least 2050</a>. That move was a <a href="https://www.industrialinfo.com/iirenergy/industry-news/article/us-threatens-to-leave-international-energy-agency-over-climate-focused-forecasts--353743">response to pressure from the U.S. government and others</a> asserting that all the IEA published forecasts did not account for rising demand from artificial intelligence data centers and anticipated accelerating adoption of green technology.</p>

<p>Assumptions rest on hard-to-predict human behavior and frequently don’t work out. The popularity of electric vehicles provides a good example. In Norway, about <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/norway-nearly-all-new-cars-sold-2024-were-fully-electric-2025-01-02/">9 in 10 new cars sold in 2024</a> were fully electric. Yet <a href="https://www.rystadenergy.com/news/norway-fuel-demand-electric-car-bus-truck-gasoline-diesel">fuel use on the roads fell only about 10%</a>, because Norwegian buses and trucks still mostly burn diesel. In China, <a href="https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/charts/electric-car-sales-in-china-2019-2024">more than half of new cars sold in 2024 were electric</a>, <a href="https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/charts/fuel-demand-and-substitution-in-china-2009-2025">but the country still uses more gasoline than it did before 2020</a>.</p>

<p>In the United States, sales of fully electric vehicles appear to have peaked, at least temporarily, following the expiration of a federal tax credit in 2025. The share of registered electric vehicles, including hybrid, plug-in and fully electric, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67885">remains in the single digits</a>. Interest, though, has climbed with pump prices: A majority of U.S. drivers now say <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/business/consumer/iran-war-gas-prices-cars-evs-hybrids-rcna266971">high gas prices have made them more open to an electric car</a>, even as the cost of buying one keeps sales down.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Electric cars sit on a street and in a parking lot." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761818/original/file-20260923-50-hsoqgt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/tesla-electric-vehicle-is-parked-in-front-of-used-electric-news-photo/2269134616">Justin Sullivan/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Preparing for the wrong problem</h2>

<p>Forecasts matter because money follows them. If demand is expected to rise, companies drill new wells, expand refineries, build tankers and construct pipelines. If demand is expected to fall, they hold back, so they don’t end up with more oil than anyone will buy at a profitable price. </p>

<p>For much of the past decade, the most influential forecasts pointed toward slowing demand. Banks grew wary of funding oil and gas projects, especially considering growing commitments to expand the use of renewable energy sources and reduce emissions to tackle climate change. <a href="https://theconversation.com/banks-retreat-from-climate-change-commitments-but-its-business-more-than-politics-265176">Banks have become more willing to support petroleum projects</a>, but funding is just the first step in the multiyear process of bringing more oil to market.</p>

<p>In addition, oil and gas fields produce less as they age. About 90% of recent spending on production went to making up for those declines, <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/the-implications-of-oil-and-gas-field-decline-rates/executive-summary">not to adding new supply beyond current production levels</a>. The result was a system built to let supply slide gently down, not to quickly ramp up.</p>

<p>Understandably, no forecast predicted a war, and with so little supply to spare, big disruptions translated into big price jumps.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An aerial view shows a large area covered by solar panels." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761828/original/file-20260923-60-b1bvmq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">It can be very hard to predict how people will react to changing energy prices and what sources they will look to for power and fuel.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/aerial-view-of-rows-of-solar-panels-covering-a-large-news-photo/2287725807">John Paraskevas/Newsday RM via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why lowering prices takes years</h2>

<p>Investments do not provide fast relief. When oil prices crashed in 2014, companies nearly stopped approving new liquefied natural gas plants to chill natural gas into liquid for shipping. </p>

<p>Demand kept growing anyway, especially in China, and <a href="https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/charts/final-investment-decisions-for-new-lng-liquefaction-capacity-2014-2025">in 2019 new investment for liquefaction capacity surged</a> – <a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/record-year-for-gas-liquefaction-investment-lights-a-path-towards-market-flexibility">a record year</a>, with about US$65 billion of investment commitments for new projects. </p>

<p>But expansion projects take years to build, so the ones skipped in the lean years simply were not there in the early 2020s. When Russia cut gas to Europe in 2022, there was <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/gas-market-lessons-from-the-2022-2023-energy-crisis/anatomy-of-a-natural-gas-crisis">no slack in the system</a>, and prices hit record highs.</p>

<p>The same delay between investment and production applies now. Money committed in 2026 won’t produce much oil and gas until the 2030s. And investors face a fresh round of guesses about <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/the-energy-transition-and-the-strait-of-hormuz">how quickly renewable energy use could grow – especially as oil prices stay high</a>. They also have to guess when the conflict might end, and when <a href="https://theconversation.com/targeting-of-energy-facilities-turned-iran-war-into-worst-case-scenario-for-gulf-states-278730">wells, refineries and shipping locations will be repaired</a> and able to resume shipping oil out of the Persian Gulf region.</p>

<p>For people filling their gas tanks and paying their heating bills, these forecasting uncertainties mean prices are likely to stay high and volatile for some time, even when the fighting stops. The energy the world has today was shaped by guesses made years ago – and the energy it will have years from now depends on the guesses being made today.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292406/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: With fuel prices at record highs, a truck driver prepares to pump diesel into a tractor trailer at a gas station in Florida
Joe Raedle/Getty Images In 2023, the International Energy Agency predicted that by 2028 the world’s oil companies would produce more oil than people wanted to buy
Prices responded to that and similar projections of slowing oil demand, dropping too low to attract investment for new wells and refineries
No forecast anticipated that the Strait of Hormuz , the main route for Middle Eastern oil to reach global markets, would be almost completely blocked
So in March 2026, when the strait closed in the wake of U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran , there was little anyone could do to quickly restore the flow of oil and gas the world’s economy depends on

Some countries did have strategic reserves, but a massive coordinated release from those supplies didn’t make a difference for long – and those reserves may need to be replenished , paradoxically increasing demand for oil in the future

Just before that conflict broke out, my fellow researcher, Hiroyasu Sakaguchi at the Institute of Energy Economics, Japan , and I wrote a report on oil and gas demand forecasts warning that even in the midst of oversupply, the global buffer for disruption is quite fragile
It was published by the Trilateral Energy Security Committee , which promotes energy-security cooperation between the U.S., Japan and South Korea

As the fighting has continued, oil prices have climbed, causing fuel shortages and raising prices not only of gasoline and diesel , but fertilizer, food , consumer goods and just about everything else
Iraq has taken to trucking oil overland to be loaded on ships in Syrian ports

Hasan Belal/Anadolu via Getty Images What an oil forecast is The reasons today’s demand and supply are so mismatched took shape years earlier, in spreadsheets that most people don’t know about or ignore
It can take about 20 years to go from exploring a new oil or gas field to shipping petroleum from it
When companies, banks and governments are deciding what projects to invest in, they look for indicators of how much oil and gas the world will want a decade or more from now
Government research agencies , oil-producing countries and big oil and gas companies all produce long-range projections of demand and supply
These projections are really sets of “what-if” stories

Forecasters start with how much energy the world uses today, then make assumptions on topics such as how fast economies will grow, how quickly new technologies like electric cars will be adopted, and how policies like those on pollution and greenhouse gas emissions will change
Each set of assumptions produces a different answer
When my colleagues and I compared major projections from 2025 for 2035 , the highest projections expected 116.6 million barrels a day would be used; the lowest expected 89.4 million barrels a day
That’s an enormous difference of 27.2 million barrels a day just 10 years out, equal to about one-quarter of all the oil the world uses today
Forecasts don’t always pan out Oil forecasts a year or two out tend to be reasonably close to reality and each other, because most of the expected production is already in motion
But much like weather forecasts, the further into the future an oil market forecast looks, the more errors are possible, both with small errors in assumptions and big surprises nobody saw coming
In the early 2000s, many experts worried the world was running out of oil that was cheap and easy to produce
Then, new drilling and hydraulic fracturing methods unlocked oil stored in layers of shale
From 2008 to 2025, U.S. production rose from 5 million barrels a day to 13.6 million
In 2022, the International Energy Agency’s main scenario had world oil demand peaking in the mid-2030s
A year later, largely because sales of electric cars were increasing so quickly, the agency moved that peak to before 2030
Then in 2025, the IEA revived a scenario it had shelved – one counting only policies already in force – in which oil demand keeps rising until at least 2050

That move was a response to pressure from the U.S. government and others asserting that all the IEA published forecasts did not account for rising demand from artificial intelligence data centers and anticipated accelerating adoption of green technology
Assumptions rest on hard-to-predict human behavior and frequently don’t work out
The popularity of electric vehicles provides a good example
In Norway, about 9 in 10 new cars sold in 2024 were fully electric
Yet fuel use on the roads fell only about 10% , because Norwegian buses and trucks still mostly burn diesel
In China, more than half of new cars sold in 2024 were electric , but the country still uses more gasoline than it did before 2020
In the United States, sales of fully electric vehicles appear to have peaked, at least temporarily, following the expiration of a federal tax credit in 2025
The share of registered electric vehicles, including hybrid, plug-in and fully electric, remains in the single digits
Interest, though, has climbed with pump prices: A majority of U.S. drivers now say high gas prices have made them more open to an electric car , even as the cost of buying one keeps sales down
Demand for electric vehicles, including used ones, has risen as fuel prices have climbed

<title>Arctic infrastructure was built on frozen ground – drones and digital twins can help spot the permafrost thaw coming</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760076/original/file-20260915-60-6fcedk.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=509%2C229%2C3030%2C2020&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A view of Wainwright, Alaska, which sits on low-lying coastal terrain underlain by permafrost.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ming Xiao</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>From the air, <a href="https://www.north-slope.org/our-communities/wainwright/">Wainwright, Alaska</a>, looks like a perfectly stable band of homes and roads between the Chukchi Sea and a vast, flat tundra. But just below the surface, the frozen ground that this town was built on contains large bodies of ice. Along the eroding coastal bluffs, that hidden ice is becoming exposed and literally melting away.</p>

<p>This is more than a landscape change. When ice within <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/kids/earth/what-is-permafrost/">frozen ground, known as permafrost</a>, melts, roads can sink, buildings can tilt, pipelines can crack and leak, and shorelines can retreat, leaving homes precariously close to the ocean’s edge. A study in 2025 estimated that permafrost thaw could cost Alaska <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02191-7">US$37 billion to $51 billion</a> just in building and road damage.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A coastal view with part of the low coastal bluff falling into the shore below." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760077/original/file-20260915-50-622acv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A coastal bluff failure in Utqiaġvik, Alaska, in August 2024 shows cracks and the narrow distance between the eroding edge and buildings.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ming Xiao</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As a civil engineer, I have spent the past decade studying how permafrost and infrastructure respond as Arctic temperatures rise <a href="https://arctic.noaa.gov/report-card/report-card-2025/surface-air-temperature-2025/">two to three times faster</a> than the global average. </p>

<p>A regional permafrost map alone cannot tell a builder how a particular foundation or road will survive as temperatures rise. Engineers need methods that can help them see beneath the surface and find the weaknesses. Using drones and digital twin technology, my colleagues and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3iRNdiYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I have been developing those techniques</a>.</p>

<h2>When frozen ground is part of the foundation</h2>

<p>Permafrost is ground that stays <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/kids/earth/what-is-permafrost/">at or below 32 degrees Fahrenheit</a> (0 degrees Celsius) for at least two consecutive years. Where permafrost is rich in ground ice, thawing can fundamentally change its ability to support infrastructure. </p>

<p>Frozen soil that has held buildings, roads and pipelines for decades can start to sink as temperatures rise and the ice that bonds soil particles weakens. When ground ice melts and water drains away, <a href="https://www.thearcticinstitute.org/permafrost-thaw-warming-world-arctic-institute-permafrost-series-fall-winter-2020/">the surface can subside</a>. The weight of homes, roads and other infrastructure can cause the ground to sink even more.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A person walks near a low bluff where a large wedge of ice is visible under the edge of the grass. The ice is melting in the water from below." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=429&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760370/original/file-20260916-50-unnwkc.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=539&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Large thawing ice wedges like this can be found in the permafrost along the Arctic coastline at Wainwright and other Alaska towns. As the ice melts, the ground can slump and erode.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Ming Xiao</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>This process is highly uneven. Locations a city block apart can contain very different amounts of ice and unfrozen water. Roads and buildings also change how snow accumulates and water drains.</p>

<p>Along the coast, thawing permafrost can leave coastal areas more vulnerable to waves and erosion. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1061/JGGEFK.GTENG-13950">Utqiaġvik, a bluff’s partial collapse</a> in 2023 and 2024 brought the bluff’s eroding edge close to roads and buildings. Waves removed material from the bottom while thaw weakened frozen ground above, causing the edge to slump.</p>

<h2>Seeing what lies beneath the tundra</h2>

<p>Much of the critical information that developers need to know before building a home or road is underground. However, drilling dense grids of boreholes in frozen soil to take samples of the ground below is expensive, disruptive and extremely labor intensive.</p>

<p>Geophysical imaging can help fill the gaps.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two scientists operate a drone over a marshy area." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760078/original/file-20260915-50-surtyn.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Researchers operate a drone-borne geophysical system over Arctic tundra near Utqiaġvik, Alaska, in August 2024. Suspending the sensor below the aircraft enables them to survey wet and thaw-sensitive ground that is hard to reach.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Emma Kappel</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>One method my team is working with is <a href="https://www.epa.gov/environmental-geophysics/very-low-frequency-electromagnetic-vlf">very low frequency electromagnetic surveying</a>, or VLF-EM. It uses electromagnetic signals from distant transmitters and measures how the ground responds. Because it does not require direct ground contact, a lightweight sensor can be carried by a drone over wetlands and tundra that are susceptible to thawing.</p>

<figure>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">How scientists and communities are monitoring Arctic permafrost.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Electromagnetic surveying is especially useful along Arctic coasts. Salty water that isn’t frozen conducts electricity much better than ice-rich frozen ground, so the differences that show up can reveal areas where the ground has thawed.</p>

<p>VLF-EM does not produce a perfect underground picture – depth estimates can be uncertain – but it <a href="https://doi.org/10.1142/S2424922X1650011X">can identify where subsurface conditions have changed</a> so engineers know where to look closely.</p>

<h2>From measurements to forecasts</h2>

<p>Infrastructure may remain in service for 20, 50 or more years, so mapping today’s underground conditions is not enough. Builders need to know what conditions are likely to look like decades into the future.</p>

<p>My research group has been working on ways to project how thaw affects two quantities that engineers care about: how much the ground settles, and how much load a foundation can support.</p>

<p>In a 2026 study, we <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-03240-5">looked at permafrost stability across Alaska’s Arctic Coastal Plain</a>, the northern coastal region that includes Prudhoe Bay and much of Alaska’s oil industry operations.</p>

<p>We found that if the world emits greenhouse gases at a high rate that continues to raise temperatures quickly, the proportion of infrastructure at risk remains below 10% around mid-century, then rises rapidly between the 2060s and 2080s. By the 2090s, about 80% of buildings, 60% of roads and 90% of pipelines are projected to be at risk of damage from sinking land.</p>

<p>We are also developing <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-are-digital-twins-a-pair-of-computer-modeling-experts-explain-181829">computer models called digital twins</a> for monitoring cold regions’ infrastructure. The digital twins replicate the real-world changing environments and aging infrastructure and can be used to predict what is likely to occur.</p>

<p>At a road embankment in Utqiaġvik, our team used fiber-optic cables to collect temperature and seismic data. In a 2026 study, we used measurements from a roughly 330-foot (100 meter) section to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2025JF008787">update a computer model</a> that combines heat-transfer physics and machine learning. As new data arrives, the digital twin adjusts to improve predictions of how permafrost temperature changes and how infrastructure performs.</p>

<p>Our goal is to use drones and geophysics to map the land, sensors to track changes, and computer models to forecast how those changes affect infrastructure.</p>

<h2>Preparing for the future</h2>

<p>Communities need easy-to-use tools showing where hazards may develop, how those hazards may change over coming decades, and what infrastructure could be affected.</p>

<p>Permafrost thaw is often described as an environmental problem. In the Arctic, it is also an engineering problem. The better that engineers can see what is happening beneath the surface – and anticipate what comes next – the more time communities have to decide where to monitor, reinforce, repair or adapt.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292097/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
